content.text: Fluids are substances that can flow and include liquids and gases. Unlike solids, fluids have no definite shape and take the shape of their container. Liquids have nearly fixed volume and a free surface; gases are compressible and expand to fill the container. Fluids offer very little resistance to shear stress. Solids and liquids are much less compressible than gases.

Pressure is the normal force per unit area. For a finite area, average pressure is Pav = F/A; locally, pressure is defined as the limiting normal force per unit area. Pressure is scalar, with dimensions [M L^-1 T^-2]. SI unit is pascal (Pa), equal to N m^-2. Common conversions: 1 atm ≈ 1.013 × 10^5 Pa; 1 bar = 10^5 Pa; 1 torr ≈ 133 Pa; 1 mm Hg ≈ 133 Pa.

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg m^-3 and dimensions are [M L^-3]. Relative density is the ratio of a substance density to the density of water at 4°C and is dimensionless. Water density at 4°C is approximately 1.0 × 10^3 kg m^-3. Liquids are nearly incompressible, whereas gas density changes substantially with pressure.

In a fluid at rest, pressure is the same at all points at the same height and acts normal to any surface. A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and the walls of its container. This principle underlies hydraulic machines.
equations: P1 = P2 (same height in a fluid at rest)

content.text: For a fluid of uniform density at rest, pressure increases with vertical depth. The pressure difference between points separated vertically by h is ρgh. For a liquid open to the atmosphere, absolute pressure at depth h is atmospheric pressure plus ρgh; gauge pressure is the excess over atmospheric pressure. Pressure at a given depth does not depend on container shape or base area.

Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 1.013 × 10^5 Pa. A mercury barometer balances atmospheric pressure against the hydrostatic pressure of a mercury column: Pa = ρgh. At sea level the mercury column is about 76 cm. The space above the column is nearly a vacuum. Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.

An open-tube manometer measures pressure difference using the difference in liquid levels in a U-tube. Gauge pressure is the difference between absolute and atmospheric pressure: Pg = P − Pa. Many practical pressure gauges report gauge pressure rather than absolute pressure.

Hydraulic machines use Pascal’s law. If two pistons of areas A1 and A2 are connected by an enclosed fluid, equal pressure gives F1/A1 = F2/A2. A larger output piston can exert a larger force, but its displacement is smaller so ideal work is conserved.

In steady flow, each fluid particle passing a point has the same velocity at that point over time. A streamline is tangent to the local velocity vector. Streamlines do not intersect because that would assign two velocities to one point. At higher speeds flow can become turbulent, with irregular velocity changes and eddies.

For steady flow, conservation of mass requires the mass passing each cross-section per unit time to be the same. For an incompressible fluid, density is constant, so the product of cross-sectional area and flow speed remains constant. Fluid speed rises in a narrower part of a pipe.

For steady flow of an ideal, incompressible, non-viscous fluid along a streamline, pressure energy, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy per unit volume sum to a constant. The principle is an application of conservation of energy and is only approximate for real viscous fluids.

Where fluid speed increases, static pressure tends to decrease along a streamline at the same height. Applications include efflux from a tank, atomisers, carburettors and dynamic lift on aircraft wings. Bernoulli’s equation should not be applied without care where viscosity, turbulence or energy input/loss is important.

For an ideal liquid flowing from a small hole at depth h below a large open liquid surface, the efflux speed is equal to the speed acquired by a freely falling body through height h. This follows from Bernoulli’s equation when the surface speed is negligible and both points are at atmospheric pressure.

Dynamic lift can arise when a moving object changes the fluid flow so that speeds and pressures differ across its surfaces. For an aircraft wing, faster flow over the upper surface can correspond to lower pressure than below, creating an upward pressure force. Real aerodynamic lift also depends on circulation, wing geometry and flow conditions.

Viscosity measures a fluid’s internal resistance to relative motion between adjacent layers. For laminar flow between parallel layers, shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient. The coefficient of viscosity η is the ratio of shear stress to rate of shear strain. Its SI unit is Pa s (or kg m^-1 s^-1). For liquids viscosity generally decreases as temperature rises; for gases it generally increases.

For laminar flow of a viscous fluid through a long cylindrical tube, volume flow rate depends on the pressure difference, tube radius to the fourth power, viscosity and tube length. Flow is strongly affected by tube radius. The law assumes steady laminar flow and suitable tube geometry.

content.text: A sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid experiences a drag force opposite its motion. Stokes’ law gives the magnitude of the drag as 6πηav, where a is sphere radius, η is fluid viscosity and v is speed. For a falling sphere, terminal velocity occurs when weight is balanced by buoyancy and viscous drag.

Molecules inside a liquid are attracted by neighbouring molecules in all directions. Molecules at the free surface have fewer neighbours and greater potential energy. Creating additional liquid surface therefore requires work. A liquid tends to minimise its surface area when other conditions permit.

Surface tension is the force per unit length acting in the plane of a liquid interface, and equivalently the surface energy per unit area. For a thin liquid film with two surfaces, a movable bar of length l experiences force F = 2Sl. Surface tension depends on the materials at the interface and generally decreases with increasing temperature.

Surface tension of a liquid-air interface can be measured by balancing the force exerted on a plate or movable bar. If extra weight mg is needed to detach a plate edge of length l from a film with two surfaces, S = mg/(2l). The factor of two accounts for the two surfaces of the film.

The angle of contact is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the contact point and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid. A small acute angle indicates wetting, as with water on clean glass; an obtuse angle indicates poor wetting, as with mercury on glass. Detergents and wetting agents reduce the contact angle.

Surface tension makes a free liquid drop spherical when gravity is negligible because a sphere has minimum area for a given volume. The pressure inside a spherical liquid drop exceeds outside pressure by 2S/r. A gas bubble in a liquid has one interface and excess pressure 2S/r; a soap bubble has two surfaces and excess pressure 4S/r.

A narrow tube can cause a wetting liquid to rise due to surface tension and the curved meniscus. For a tube radius a, liquid density ρ and contact angle θ, the rise height is h = 2S cosθ/(ρga). Capillary rise increases as tube radius decreases. If cosθ is negative, as for a non-wetting liquid, the liquid level is depressed.

The upper body mass supported by two femurs is 40 kg and each femur has cross-sectional area 10 cm². Taking g = 10 m s^-2, total area is 20 × 10^-4 m² and force is 400 N, giving average pressure 2 × 10^5 Pa.

For a swimmer 10 m below a lake surface, using water density 1000 kg m^-3, g = 10 m s^-2 and atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10^5 Pa, the absolute pressure is approximately 2.01 × 10^5 Pa, about two atmospheres.

The chapter includes a worked example using pressure at a known depth to determine a fluid’s density. The governing relationship is the hydrostatic pressure equation; ensure the pressure is interpreted as absolute or gauge as appropriate.
At large ocean depths, hydrostatic pressure increases by approximately ρgh above atmospheric pressure. The chapter example illustrates the large pressures that deep-ocean structures must withstand.

Two syringes connected by a fluid transmit pressure according to Pascal’s law. The force on each piston is proportional to its cross-sectional area, while piston displacements vary inversely with area for an incompressible fluid.

A hydraulic car lift uses pressure transmission to raise a load. The pressure generated by the smaller piston is transmitted through the fluid and acts on the larger piston; force multiplication depends on the ratio of piston areas.

The chapter includes a worked aircraft-lift example based on different air speeds above and below a wing. Bernoulli’s principle relates the pressure difference to the difference in dynamic pressure; multiplying pressure difference by wing area gives an idealised lift estimate.

A block slides over a liquid film while pulled by a hanging mass. At constant speed, the pull equals the hanging weight. The shear stress is force divided by contact area, and the strain rate is speed divided by film thickness; their ratio gives viscosity.

For a sphere falling at terminal speed through oil, Stokes’ law and force balance give η = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9vt). The chapter example uses a copper sphere radius 2.0 mm, terminal speed 6.5 cm s^-1, copper density 8.9 × 10^3 kg m^-3 and oil density 1.5 × 10^3 kg m^-3, obtaining viscosity about 0.99 Pa s.

The chapter example asks for the pressure needed to form a hemispherical bubble at the end of a capillary immersed in water. Pressure outside includes atmospheric pressure plus hydrostatic pressure; the bubble excess pressure is 2S/r because it has one liquid-gas interface.

content.text: Key relationships: pressure P = F/A; hydrostatic pressure P = Pa + ρgh; continuity A v = constant for incompressible steady flow; Bernoulli P + ½ρv² + ρgy = constant for ideal flow. Pascal’s law explains hydraulic machines.

Viscosity relates shear stress to rate of shear strain; Stokes’ drag on a sphere is F = 6πηav. Surface tension is force per unit length or surface energy per unit area. Surface tension explains spherical drops, excess pressure in drops/bubbles and capillary rise.

Pressure is scalar even though defined using force per area, because the relevant force is the normal component. Pressure exists throughout a fluid, not only at walls. The formula P = Pa + ρgh assumes a fluid of uniform density. Gauge pressure is absolute pressure minus atmospheric pressure. Streamlines do not intersect. Bernoulli’s principle neglects viscous energy losses.

content.text: As temperature rises, liquid molecules become more mobile and liquid viscosity usually falls. In gases, increased molecular motion generally increases viscosity. Surface tension usually decreases as temperature rises because surface molecules have less excess cohesive effect.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.1: Explain why (a) The blood pressure in humans is greater at the feet than at the brain (b) Atmospheric pressure at a height of about 6 km decreases to nearly half of its value at the sea level, though the height of the atmosphere is more than 100 km (c) Hydrostatic pressure is a scalar quantity even though pressure is force divided by area.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.2: Explain why (a) The angle of contact of mercury with glass is obtuse, while that of water with glass is acute. (b) Water on a clean glass surface tends to spread out while mercury on the same surface tends to form drops. (Put differently, water wets glass while mercury does not.)

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.3: Fill in the blanks using the word(s) from the list appended with each statement: (a) Surface tension of liquids generally . . . with temperatures (increases / decreases) (b) Viscosity of gases . . . with temperature, whereas viscosity of liquids . . . with temperature (increases / decreases) (c) For solids with elastic modulus of rigidity, the shearing force is proportional to . . . , while for fluids it is proportional to . . . (shear strain / rate of shear strain) (d) For a fluid in a steady flow, the increase in flow speed at a constriction follows (conservation of mass / Bernoulli’s principle) (e) For the model of a plane in a wind tunnel, turbulence occurs at a ... speed for turbulence for an actual plane (greater / smaller)

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.4: Explain why (a) To keep a piece of paper horizontal, you should blow over, not under, it (b) When we try to close a water tap with our fingers, fast jets of water gush through the openings between our fingers (c) The size of the needle of a syringe controls flow rate better than the thumb pressure exerted by a doctor while administering an injection (d) A fluid flowing out of a small hole in a vessel results in a backward thrust on the vessel (e) A spinning cricket ball in air does not follow a parabolic trajectory

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.5: A 50 kg girl wearing high heel shoes balances on a single heel. The heel is circular with a diameter 1.0 cm. What is the pressure exerted by the heel on the horizontal floor ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.6: Toricelli’s barometer used mercury. Pascal duplicated it using French wine of density 984 kg m–3. Determine the height of the wine column for normal atmospheric pressure.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.7: A vertical off-shore structure is built to withstand a maximum stress of 109 Pa. Is the structure suitable for putting up on top of an oil well in the ocean ? Take the depth of the ocean to be roughly 3 km, and ignore ocean currents.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.8: A hydraulic automobile lift is designed to lift cars with a maximum mass of 3000 kg. The area of cross-section of the piston carrying the load is 425 cm2. What maximum pressure would the smaller piston have to bear ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.9: A U-tube contains water and methylated spirit separated by mercury. The mercury columns in the two arms are in level with 10.0 cm of water in one arm and 12.5 cm of spirit in the other. What is the specific gravity of spirit ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.10: In the previous problem, if 15.0 cm of water and spirit each are further poured into the respective arms of the tube, what is the difference in the levels of mercury in the two arms ? (Specific gravity of mercury = 13.6)
NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.11: Can Bernoulli’s equation be used to describe the flow of water through a rapid in a river ? Explain.
NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.12: Does it matter if one uses gauge instead of absolute pressures in applying Bernoulli’s equation ? Explain.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.13: Glycerine flows steadily through a horizontal tube of length 1.5 m and radius 1.0 cm. If the amount of glycerine collected per second at one end is 4.0 × 10–3 kg s–1, what is the pressure difference between the two ends of the tube ? (Density of glycerine = 1.3 × 103 kg m–3 and viscosity of glycerine = 0.83 Pa s). [You may also like to check if the assumption of laminar flow in the tube is correct].

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.14: In a test experiment on a model aeroplane in a wind tunnel, the flow speeds on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing are 70 m s–1and 63 m s-1 respectively. What is the lift on the wing if its area is 2.5 m2 ? Take the density of air to be 1.3 kg m–3.
NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.15: Figures 9.20(a) and (b) refer to the steady flow of a (non-viscous) liquid. Which of the two figures is incorrect ? Why ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.16: The cylindrical tube of a spray pump has a cross-section of 8.0 cm2 one end of which has 40 fine holes each of diameter 1.0 mm. If the liquid flow inside the tube is 1.5 m min–1, what is the speed of ejection of the liquid through the holes ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.17: A U-shaped wire is dipped in a soap solution, and removed. The thin soap film formed between the wire and the light slider supports a weight of 1.5 × 10–2 N (which includes the small weight of the slider). The length of the slider is 30 cm. What is the surface tension of the film ?

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.18: Figure 9.21 (a) shows a thin liquid film supporting a small weight = 4.5 × 10–2 N. What is the weight supported by a film of the same liquid at the same temperature in Fig. (b) and (c) ? Explain your answer physically.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.19: What is the pressure inside the drop of mercury of radius 3.00 mm at room temperature ? Surface tension of mercury at that temperature (20 °C) is 4.65 × 10–1 N m–1. The atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 105 Pa. Also give the excess pressure inside the drop.

NCERT Chapter 9 exercise 9.20: What is the excess pressure inside a bubble of soap solution of radius 5.00 mm, given that the surface tension of soap solution at the temperature (20 °C) is 2.50 × 10–2 N m–1 ? If an air bubble of the same dimension were formed at depth of 40.0 cm inside a container containing the soap solution (of relative density 1.20), what would be the pressure inside the bubble ? (1 atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 105 Pa).
